subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Chemical cells and solar cells compared
Current as a flow of charge
Potential difference as work per unit charge
Ohmic and non-ohmic behaviour, and heating
Resistors in series and in parallel
Emf, internal resistance and terminal pd

questions.q: A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. What does this mean?
options: The cell holds a store of 1.5 C of charge, which it releases into the circuit.
The cell pushes each coulomb of charge around the circuit with a force of 1.5 N.
For each coulomb passing through the cell, 1.5 J is transferred to electrical energy.
The cell drives a current of 1.5 A through any circuit connected to it.
optionWhy: A student who pictures a cell as a container of charge picks this. The volt is a joule per coulomb, not a quantity of charge, and a cell stores no charge: the carriers are already in the circuit and the cell does work on them.
A student who takes the name 'electromotive force' literally picks this. Emf is energy per unit charge, measured in J C⁻¹ (volts), not a force measured in newtons.

Emf is the work done by the source per unit charge, ε = W/q, and 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹. So 1.5 J of chemical energy is transferred to electrical energy for every coulomb that the cell moves around the circuit.
A student who thinks a cell supplies a fixed current picks this. The emf is in volts, not amperes, and the current the cell drives depends on the total resistance of the circuit: I = ε/(R + r).
questions.explain: Emf is the work done by the source per unit charge, ε = W/q, and 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹. So 1.5 J of chemical energy is transferred to electrical energy for every coulomb that the cell moves around the circuit.
questions.working: ε = W/q, so the energy transferred per coulomb is W = εq = 1.5 V × 1 C = 1.5 J (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

questions.q: A chemical cell and a solar cell are each used as the energy source in a circuit. Which describes the main energy transfer in each?
options: Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: energy of light to electrical.
Chemical cell: stored electrical energy is let out. Solar cell: light to electrical.
Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: the Sun's heat to electrical.
Chemical cell: chemical energy to electrical. Solar cell: its stored light to electrical.
optionWhy: In a chemical cell, reactions transfer the chemical energy of the reactants to electrical energy. In a photovoltaic solar cell, the energy of the incident light (electromagnetic radiation) is transferred directly to electrical energy.

A student who thinks a battery is a store of 'electricity' picks this. A chemical cell stores chemical energy in its reactants; electrical energy is produced only while the reactions run with a current in the circuit.
A student who confuses solar cells with solar water-heating panels picks this. A photovoltaic cell responds to light, not heat: the energy of the light frees charge carriers and produces an emf.
A student who thinks a solar cell stores the light it absorbs, like a battery, picks this. A solar cell stores nothing; it transfers light energy to electrical energy only while light falls on it.
questions.explain: In a chemical cell, reactions transfer the chemical energy of the reactants to electrical energy. In a photovoltaic solar cell, the energy of the incident light (electromagnetic radiation) is transferred directly to electrical energy.

questions.q: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the pd across it, but connects the meters the wrong way round. The circuit is: a cell, a voltmeter and the lamp connected in series in a single loop, with an ammeter connected in parallel with the lamp. Both meters are ideal. What does the student observe?
options: The lamp is off and both meters read zero, as there is no current in the circuit.
The lamp is off, the ammeter reads zero and the voltmeter reads the emf of the cell.
The ammeter short-circuits the lamp, so a very large current flows through the ammeter.
The lamp lights normally, and the meters show its current and pd as when correctly connected.
optionWhy: A student who thinks that a pd needs a current picks this. The ammeter does read zero, but a pd exists across the voltmeter even though no charge flows through it: by the loop rule, the emf must appear somewhere, and the only place is across the voltmeter's (infinite) resistance.

An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, so with it in series there is no current in the loop: the lamp is off and the ammeter reads zero. With no current, there is no pd across the lamp (or the ammeter) and no pd across any internal resistance, so the whole emf appears across the voltmeter.

A student who looks only at the ammeter–lamp pair picks this. The ammeter does bypass the lamp, but the voltmeter's infinite resistance is in series with the whole loop, so the current is zero. A short circuit gives a large current only if the rest of the loop has low resistance.

A student who treats meters as passive readers that work wherever they are placed picks this. An ideal voltmeter in series acts as a break in the circuit, and an ideal ammeter in parallel acts as a zero-resistance bypass, so the circuit is changed completely.
questions.explain: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, so with it in series there is no current in the loop: the lamp is off and the ammeter reads zero. With no current, there is no pd across the lamp (or the ammeter) and no pd across any internal resistance, so the whole emf appears across the voltmeter.

questions.q: The circuit diagram shows two lamps, L₁ and L₂, of different resistances connected in parallel to a cell, together with ammeters A₁ and A₂. Which statement about the ammeter readings is correct?
options: A₁ and A₂ give the same reading, because the current is the same at every point in the circuit.
A₂ reads exactly half of A₁, because the current splits into equal parts at a junction.
A₁ reads more than A₂, because A₁ measures the total current and A₂ measures only the current in L₂.
A₂ reads less than A₁, because L₂ uses up some of the current passing through it.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the current is the same everywhere in any circuit picks this. That is true only in a single loop; here the current divides at the junction, and A₂ measures only the part that goes through L₂.

A student who thinks a junction always splits the current equally picks this. The lamps have different resistances, so the branch with the smaller resistance takes the larger share; A₂ reads half only if the lamps are identical.

A₁ is in the single wire before the junction, so it reads the total current. A₂ is in the branch with L₂ only, so it reads the current in L₂. At the junction I = I₁ + I₂, so A₁ − A₂ is the current in L₁.

A student who thinks current is consumed by a lamp picks this. A₂ does read less, but because the current divided at the junction, not because L₂ used any up: the current leaving L₂ equals the current entering it.
questions.explain: A₁ is in the single wire before the junction, so it reads the total current. A₂ is in the branch with L₂ only, so it reads the current in L₂. At the junction I = I₁ + I₂, so A₁ − A₂ is the current in L₁.

questions.q: A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?
options: Free electrons drift slowly, in the opposite direction to the conventional current.
Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
Protons move along the wire, in the same direction as the conventional current.
Electrons leave the cell and some are used up in the lamp, so fewer return to the cell.
optionWhy: In a metal the charge carriers are free (delocalized) electrons. Being negative, they drift from the negative towards the positive terminal, opposite to the conventional current, and their drift speed is small (typically well under 1 mm s⁻¹).

A student who thinks the electrons race round the circuit picks this. The electrons drift slowly; the lamp lights at once because the electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, so carriers everywhere start moving together.

A student who thinks conventional current is a flow of positive charges picks this. In a metal the positive charges are in the nuclei of the lattice ions, which stay in place; only electrons move along the wire.

A student who thinks current is used up in components picks this. Charge is conserved: the current is the same all round a series loop. The lamp transfers energy from the carriers, not the carriers themselves.
questions.explain: In a metal the charge carriers are free (delocalized) electrons. Being negative, they drift from the negative towards the positive terminal, opposite to the conventional current, and their drift speed is small (typically well under 1 mm s⁻¹).

questions.q: A steady current of 0.50 A flows through a small electric motor for 2.0 minutes. In this time, 360 J of energy is transferred from electrical energy to other forms in the motor. What is the potential difference across the motor?
optionWhy: A student who leaves the time in minutes gets q = 0.50 × 2.0 = 1.0 C and V = 360 V. The time must be in seconds, 120 s, before finding the charge.
A student who uses the current as if it were the charge gets 360/0.50 = 720 V. The charge is the current multiplied by the time: q = 0.50 A × 120 s = 60 C.
A student who thinks pd is energy per second gets 360/120 = 3.0. That is the power, 3.0 W. Potential difference is energy per unit charge, V = W/q.
The charge that passes is q = It = 0.50 × 120 = 60 C. V = W/q = 360/60 = 6.0 V: 6.0 J is transferred for each coulomb passing through the motor.
questions.explain: The charge that passes is q = It = 0.50 × 120 = 60 C. V = W/q = 360/60 = 6.0 V: 6.0 J is transferred for each coulomb passing through the motor.

questions.q: Copper is a good electrical conductor and polythene is an insulator. Which statement explains the difference?
options: Copper contains charged particles, but polythene contains no charged particles at all.
Copper has protons that are free to move; polythene's protons are all held in place.
Copper has electrons free to move through it; polythene's electrons are bound to its molecules.
Copper lets the charge stored in a cell pass through; polythene blocks this charge.
optionWhy: A student who thinks insulators have no charges picks this. Polythene, like all matter, contains protons and electrons; they are simply not free to move.

A student who thinks conventional current is a flow of positive charges picks this. The protons in copper are in the nuclei of the lattice ions and do not move along the wire; the mobile carriers are electrons.

Conduction needs mobile charge carriers. In copper, some electrons are delocalized and free to move through the lattice; in polythene every electron is held in a bond or an atom, so almost no carriers can move.

A student who thinks a cell supplies charge from a store picks this. The charge carriers are part of the conductor itself; a cell provides energy, not charge. Polythene does not conduct because its own electrons cannot move.
questions.explain: Conduction needs mobile charge carriers. In copper, some electrons are delocalized and free to move through the lattice; in polythene every electron is held in a bond or an atom, so almost no carriers can move.

questions.q: What is the origin of the electrical resistance of a metal wire?
options: Free electrons collide with the vibrating lattice ions, transferring energy to them.
Some of the free electrons are absorbed by the metal atoms, so fewer leave than enter.
The electrons rub against the surface of the wire, like water flowing along a pipe.
The electrons bump into one another as they crowd through the wire.
optionWhy: As the free electrons drift under the electric field, they collide with the positive ions of the lattice, which are vibrating about fixed positions. Each collision transfers energy to the lattice, opposing the drift and heating the metal.

A student who thinks current is used up picks this. Charge is conserved, so as many electrons leave a section of wire each second as enter it. Resistance transfers energy from the electrons; it does not remove them.

A student who extends the water-in-pipes analogy too far picks this. The current flows through the whole cross-section of the metal, and resistance arises from collisions with lattice ions throughout its volume, which is why R ∝ L/A.

A student who uses a crowd or traffic-jam picture picks this. In the IB model, the energy is transferred to the metal through collisions of electrons with the massive lattice ions, not with each other.
questions.explain: As the free electrons drift under the electric field, they collide with the positive ions of the lattice, which are vibrating about fixed positions. Each collision transfers energy to the lattice, opposing the drift and heating the metal.

questions.q: The I–V characteristic of a filament lamp is plotted with current I on the vertical axis and pd V on the horizontal axis. Up to 0.10 V the graph is a straight line through the origin, and at 0.10 V the current is 0.050 A. At 6.0 V the current is 0.50 A, and the tangent to the curve at this point has a gradient of 0.040 A V⁻¹. What is the resistance of the lamp at 6.0 V, and how is it found?
options: 25 Ω, from the reciprocal of the tangent's gradient
2.0 Ω, from V/I on the straight part near the origin
0.040 Ω, from the gradient of the tangent at 6.0 V
12 Ω, from V/I using the pd and current at 6.0 V
optionWhy: A student who thinks resistance is the inverse gradient of the I–V graph gets 1/0.040 = 25 Ω. That method works only for a straight line through the origin; for a curve, R = V/I at the point.

A student who thinks a component has one fixed resistance gets 0.10/0.050 = 2.0 Ω. That is the resistance of the cold filament. The filament heats up at higher pd, and its resistance at 6.0 V is much larger.
A student who reads the gradient of an I–V graph directly as a resistance gets 0.040. With I on the vertical axis the gradient has units A V⁻¹, not Ω; and in any case resistance is V/I at the point.
Resistance is defined as R = V/I at the operating point, for any component: R = 6.0 V / 0.50 A = 12 Ω. The tangent's gradient describes how the current changes with pd, not the resistance.
questions.explain: Resistance is defined as R = V/I at the operating point, for any component: R = 6.0 V / 0.50 A = 12 Ω. The tangent's gradient describes how the current changes with pd, not the resistance.
questions.working: R = V/I at the point = 6.0 V / 0.50 A = 12 Ω.

questions.q: A copper cable has length 5.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm. The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is the resistance of the cable?
optionWhy: A student who uses the diameter as the radius gets A = π × (1.0 × 10⁻³)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁶ m², four times too large, and R = 2.7 × 10⁻² Ω. The radius is half the diameter, 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m.
A student who works out A = π × 0.50² = 0.785 mm² and converts with 10⁻³ gets A = 7.85 × 10⁻⁴ m² and R = 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ Ω. Since 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², so A = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m².
A student who forgets to square the radius gets A = π × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.57 × 10⁻³ and R = 5.4 × 10⁻⁵ Ω. The cross-sectional area is πr², so the radius must be squared.

questions.q: Which is a statement of Ohm's law?
options: The current in a conductor is proportional to the pd across it, provided its temperature is constant.
Every conductor obeys V = IR, so the current in any conductor is proportional to the pd.
The resistance of a conductor is proportional to the pd across it, at constant temperature.
The current in a conductor is proportional to the power supplied to it, at constant temperature.
optionWhy: Ohm's law states that the current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided physical conditions such as temperature stay the same. A metal conductor at constant temperature obeys it.

A student who thinks V = IR is Ohm's law picks this. V = IR only defines resistance and applies to any component; the current is proportional to the pd only if R stays constant, which is not true of, for example, a filament lamp.
A student who reads R = V/I as saying that R depends on V picks this. For a conductor obeying Ohm's law, doubling V doubles I, so R = V/I stays the same.

A student who mixes up pd with power (energy per second) picks this. Ohm's law relates current to pd, the energy per unit charge. For an ohmic conductor P = I²R, so the power is proportional to the square of the current, not to the current.
questions.explain: Ohm's law states that the current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided physical conditions such as temperature stay the same. A metal conductor at constant temperature obeys it.

questions.q: Three components X, Y and Z are tested. The currents at pds of 1.0 V, 2.0 V and 4.0 V are: X — 0.10 A, 0.20 A, 0.40 A; Y — 0.05 A, 0.15 A, 0.35 A; Z — 0.20 A, 0.30 A, 0.40 A. Which of the components are ohmic, and why?
options: X and Y: each gives a straight-line graph of I against V.
None of them: V/I should double as V doubles, and does not.
X only: V/I has the same value at every reading.
X, Y and Z: V = IR applies to every one of the readings.
optionWhy: A student who thinks any straight-line graph means ohmic picks this. Y's line (I = 0.10V − 0.05) does not pass through the origin, so V/I changes with V and Y is non-ohmic.

A student who reads R = V/I as 'resistance is proportional to pd', and takes that to be Ohm's law, expects V/I to double when V doubles, and no component does this. Ohm's law says I ∝ V, so V/I stays constant. X has V/I = 10 Ω at every reading, so X is ohmic; Y (20 Ω, 13 Ω, 11 Ω) and Z (5.0 Ω, 6.7 Ω, 10 Ω) are not.

For X, V/I = 10 Ω at every reading, so I ∝ V: X is ohmic. For Y, V/I is 20 Ω, 13 Ω and 11 Ω; its graph is a straight line that does not pass through the origin. For Z, V/I is 5.0 Ω, 6.7 Ω and 10 Ω. Neither Y nor Z has I proportional to V.
A student who thinks Ohm's law is V = IR picks this. Resistance can be calculated for any component at any pd; Ohm's law requires that this V/I stays the same as V changes, which is true only for X.
questions.explain: For X, V/I = 10 Ω at every reading, so I ∝ V: X is ohmic. For Y, V/I is 20 Ω, 13 Ω and 11 Ω; its graph is a straight line that does not pass through the origin. For Z, V/I is 5.0 Ω, 6.7 Ω and 10 Ω. Neither Y nor Z has I proportional to V.

questions.q: As the pd across a filament lamp is increased, the ratio V/I for the lamp increases. Which explanation is correct?
options: More of the current is used up in the filament at higher pd, so less passes through it.
The filament heats up; its ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often.
The filament expands as it heats up, and its extra length increases its resistance.
At higher current the electrons crowd together and collide with one another more.
optionWhy: A student who thinks current is used up picks this. The current into the filament equals the current out; charge is conserved. The ratio V/I rises because the resistance of the hot filament increases.

The current heats the filament (the heating effect of a current). At a higher temperature the lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude, electron–ion collisions become more frequent, and the resistance V/I increases.

A student who explains the rise with R = ρL/A and expansion picks this. Expansion increases the area as well as the length and is only about 1%; the resistance rises several-fold because the resistivity increases with temperature.

A student who uses a crowd picture of resistance picks this. Resistance arises from electron collisions with the lattice ions, and it rises here because those ions vibrate more at the higher temperature.
questions.explain: The current heats the filament (the heating effect of a current). At a higher temperature the lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude, electron–ion collisions become more frequent, and the resistance V/I increases.

questions.q: A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
optionWhy: A student who forgets to square the current uses P = IR = 0.25 × 24 = 6.0 and gets 6.0 × 120 = 720 J. IR is the pd (6.0 V), not the power; P = I²R.
A student who leaves the time in minutes gets 1.5 × 2.0 = 3.0 J. The watt is a joule per second, so t = 120 s.
A student who takes power to be the energy gives the power, 1.5 W, as 1.5 J. Power is energy per second; the energy is E = Pt = 1.5 W × 120 s.

questions.q: A 12 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current in the 12 Ω resistor?
optionWhy: The parallel pair has 1/R_p = 1/6.0 + 1/12, so R_p = 4.0 Ω; the total resistance is 4.0 + 4.0 = 8.0 Ω and the supply current is 12/8.0 = 1.5 A. The pd across the parallel pair is 1.5 × 4.0 = 6.0 V, so the current in the 12 Ω resistor is 6.0/12 = 0.50 A.

A student who splits the 1.5 A supply current equally between the branches gets 0.75 A. The branches have the same pd, 6.0 V, so the current divides in inverse proportion to resistance: 1.0 A in the 6.0 Ω resistor and 0.50 A in the 12 Ω resistor.
A student who puts the full supply pd across the 12 Ω resistor gets 12/12 = 1.0 A. The 4.0 Ω series resistor takes 6.0 V of the 12 V, leaving 6.0 V across the parallel pair.
A student who thinks the current is the same everywhere in a circuit gives the supply current, 1.5 A. At the junction the current divides, so each branch carries only part of it.
questions.explain: The parallel pair has 1/R_p = 1/6.0 + 1/12, so R_p = 4.0 Ω; the total resistance is 4.0 + 4.0 = 8.0 Ω and the supply current is 12/8.0 = 1.5 A. The pd across the parallel pair is 1.5 × 4.0 = 6.0 V, so the current in the 12 Ω resistor is 6.0/12 = 0.50 A.

questions.q: Two identical filament lamps P and Q are connected in series with a cell of negligible internal resistance, in the order: positive terminal, lamp P, lamp Q, negative terminal. How do the brightnesses of the lamps compare?
options: They are equally bright, and each is as bright as a single lamp on the cell.
P is brighter, since some of the current is used up in P before it reaches Q.
Q is brighter, as the electrons leave the negative terminal and so reach Q first.
They are equally bright, and each is dimmer than a single lamp on the cell.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the cell supplies a fixed current picks this. The current depends on the total resistance: with two lamps in series the resistance is larger and the current smaller, so each lamp is dimmer than a single lamp.
A student who thinks current is used up in components picks this. Charge is conserved: the current is the same at every point in a series loop, so P and Q carry equal currents.

A student who reasons sequentially, following the electrons round the loop, picks this. The current in a series loop is set by the whole circuit and is the same everywhere; the order of the lamps makes no difference.

In series the current is the same in both lamps (I = I₁ = I₂), and identical lamps carrying the same current have the same pd and the same power, so they are equally bright. The two lamps share the supply pd, so each has less pd and less current than one lamp alone, and each is dimmer.
questions.explain: In series the current is the same in both lamps (I = I₁ = I₂), and identical lamps carrying the same current have the same pd and the same power, so they are equally bright. The two lamps share the supply pd, so each has less pd and less current than one lamp alone, and each is dimmer.

questions.q: A battery of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal potential difference of the battery?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the terminal pd always equals the emf gives 9.0 V. There is a current in the internal resistance, so a pd Ir = 1.0 V is dropped inside the battery.

A student who finds the current from the external resistance alone gets I = 9.0/4.0 = 2.25 A and V = 9.0 − 2.25 × 0.50 = 7.9 V. The internal resistance is in series in the loop, so I = ε/(R + r) = 2.0 A.
A student who gives the pd across the internal resistance, Ir = 2.0 × 0.50 = 1.0 V, as the terminal pd picks this. That pd is dissipated inside the battery; the terminal pd is what is left, 8.0 V.
ε = I(R + r), so I = 9.0/(4.0 + 0.50) = 2.0 A. The terminal pd is V = IR = 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0 V (equivalently, ε − Ir = 9.0 − 1.0 = 8.0 V).
questions.explain: ε = I(R + r), so I = 9.0/(4.0 + 0.50) = 2.0 A. The terminal pd is V = IR = 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0 V (equivalently, ε − Ir = 9.0 − 1.0 = 8.0 V).

questions.q: The graph shows how the terminal pd V of a cell varies with the current I that it delivers. What is the internal resistance of the cell?
optionWhy: A student who takes the terminal pd to be the pd across the internal resistance divides 1.0 V by 2.5 A to get 0.40 Ω. The terminal pd is the pd across the external circuit; the pd across r is the lost volts, ε − V = 0.50 V.
A student who divides the emf by the current gets 1.5/2.5 = 0.60 Ω. That is the total resistance R + r of the whole circuit at this current, not the internal resistance on its own.
Rearranging ε = I(R + r) gives V = ε − Ir, so the magnitude of the gradient is r. The line falls from 1.5 V to 1.0 V as the current rises from 0 to 2.5 A: r = 0.50 V / 2.5 A = 0.20 Ω.
A student who reads the fall in terminal pd, 1.5 − 1.0 = 0.50 V, as the internal resistance picks this. The lost volts are Ir; dividing by the current, 2.5 A, gives r = 0.20 Ω.
questions.explain: Rearranging ε = I(R + r) gives V = ε − Ir, so the magnitude of the gradient is r. The line falls from 1.5 V to 1.0 V as the current rises from 0 to 2.5 A: r = 0.50 V / 2.5 A = 0.20 Ω.
questions.working: V = ε − Ir, so the graph of V against I is a straight line with intercept ε and gradient −r. Intercept: ε = 1.5 V. At I = 2.5 A, V = 1.0 V, so r = (ε − V)/I = (1.5 − 1.0)/2.5 = 0.20 Ω.

questions.q: An NTC thermistor is warmed, and separately a light-dependent resistor (LDR) is moved into brighter light. How does the resistance of each change?
options: The thermistor's rises, as in a hot metal wire; the LDR's falls.
Both fall, since more charge carriers are released in each device.
The thermistor's falls; the LDR's rises, as it resists brighter light.
Neither changes, since a component's resistance is a fixed property.
optionWhy: A student who generalizes the behaviour of metals to every resistor picks this. A metal's resistance does rise with temperature, but an NTC thermistor is a semiconductor: warming it releases more charge carriers, so its resistance falls.
Both are semiconductor devices. Raising the temperature of an NTC thermistor, or the light intensity on an LDR, releases more charge carriers, so the resistance of each decreases.
A student who reads 'light-dependent resistor' as 'resists light' picks this. Light releases charge carriers in the LDR, so the brighter the light, the lower its resistance.
A student who thinks every component has one fixed resistance picks this. Thermistors and LDRs are variable resistors: their resistance changes with temperature and with light intensity respectively.
questions.explain: Both are semiconductor devices. Raising the temperature of an NTC thermistor, or the light intensity on an LDR, releases more charge carriers, so the resistance of each decreases.

questions.q: A potentiometer has a uniform resistance track connected across a 9.0 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected between one end of the track and the sliding contact, which is one third of the way along the track from that end. What does the voltmeter read?
optionWhy: The two parts of the track are in series and carry the same current, so the pd divides in proportion to resistance. The part between the end and the slider has one third of the track's resistance, so its pd is 9.0 × 1/3 = 3.0 V.
A student who thinks the full supply pd appears across any part of a circuit gives 9.0 V. The pds across the two parts of the track add up to 9.0 V, so each part has only a share.
A student who thinks the pd is always shared equally between series parts gives 4.5 V. The pd divides in proportion to resistance, and the parts are in the ratio 1 : 2.

A student who thinks the smaller resistance takes the larger share of the pd gives 9.0 × 2/3 = 6.0 V. In series, the same current flows through both parts, so V = IR is larger across the larger resistance.
questions.explain: The two parts of the track are in series and carry the same current, so the pd divides in proportion to resistance. The part between the end and the slider has one third of the track's resistance, so its pd is 9.0 × 1/3 = 3.0 V.
questions.working: The section of track between the end and the slider has 1/3 of the total resistance. Series parts share the pd in proportion to resistance: V = 9.0 V × 1/3 = 3.0 V.
